passage: In second year, my friend Afreen went quiet for almost a month. She skipped the canteen, stopped replying in our group chat, and I decided it was because of me. That October I'd forgotten her birthday by a day. I felt so guilty that the guilt itself seemed like proof: nobody feels this bad unless they've done something bad. I, Zubin, wrote her three long apology messages. She answered the third with just, 'Why are you sorry?' Later she told me her parents were going through a rough patch and she'd been going home every weekend. My birthday slip had barely registered. Looking back, the guilt wasn't useless. It told me how much the friendship mattered. It just wasn't evidence. What she needed was someone to sit with her, not someone apologising.

Note, college counselling cell, Wednesday
Alka, second-year B.Com, came in during lunch. Her roommate has been low for two weeks, sleeping late and missing classes, and Alka is convinced it is her fault. 'I complained about the music one night. I feel sick with guilt, so I must have caused it.' She listed other 'evidence': she got the better bed by the window, she has more friends on the floor. We talked about asking the roommate kindly how she is doing, and mentioning that the counselling cell is open to her too. Alka left calmer. I have asked the warden to keep a gentle eye on the roommate, and Alka will check in with me on Friday.
Jasleen, counsellor

Girls' hostel, Sunday, 11 p.m.

Sangeeta has been so low this week. She barely comes to mess, she's always in bed with her headphones in, and she said "I'm fine" in that flat way four times.

And I'm sure it's me. On Monday I got the window-side bed in the new room when she wanted it. On Wednesday I forgot to save her dinner. I feel horribly guilty, and the guilt feels like proof. Why else would I feel this bad unless I did it?

I wrote her an apology note and then tore it up, because what exactly am I apologising for?

Tonight, while brushing my teeth, she said, not really to me, "I didn't get the scholarship." That's it. She said she's talking to the counsellor on Tuesday.

So maybe the guilt wasn't evidence. Maybe it just means I care about her a lot. I want to be a good roommate this week, not a sorry one.

— Lakshmi

qa.a: "I didn't get the scholarship."

qa.a: The guilt was strong and she could find small things she had done, like the bed and the dinner, so the feeling seemed to point to her. Feeling that bad seemed impossible unless she was to blame.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi do this week instead of apologising?
qa.a: She could simply be around for Sangeeta, save her dinner, and ask gently if she wants company before Tuesday. Caring actions fit better than an apology for something she didn't cause.

qa.q: What is this week likely like for Sangeeta?
qa.a: Sangeeta is dealing with the scholarship disappointment and probably has little energy for anyone. A roommate full of guilty apologies might feel like one more thing to handle.

grounding: A student feels guilty about her roommate's low mood and assumes she caused it, then realises the guilt reflects how much she cares, not wrongdoing.
